# EO 14365 — Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence

> **Federal policy, not NASA governance: binding on agencies as federal policy, a separate
> question from what NASA's own directives require.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary.
> It never by itself establishes what a specific NASA directive requires, and must not be
> cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | The President (Executive Office of the President) |
| **Kind** | Executive Order |
| **Status** | Signed December 11, 2025 [p.3, dateline]; Federal Register publication date December 16, 2025, cited as 90 FR 58499 (that page-number form is cited as reported and was not independently checked). Currently in force; it is newer than EO 14179 and does not revoke it. |
| **Where to get it** | Federal Register / govinfo.gov, free public (citation 90 FR 58499 — verify). Public copy, confirmed anonymously off-network on 2026-10-26: `https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-12-16/html/2025-23092.htm` |
| **Binds whom** | Primarily executive-branch officials with named duties: the Attorney General (Sec. 3), the Secretary of Commerce (Sec. 4-5), "Executive departments and agencies" generally for discretionary-grant conditions (Sec. 5(b)), the Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (Sec. 6), and the Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission (Sec. 7) |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** (our reading) This is a federal-versus-state regulatory order, not an agency-internal AI governance document — it is about which level of government may regulate AI providers and users, not about how a federal agency like NASA should manage its own AI use. Its relationship to OMB M-25-21's agency-level obligations is unresolved by this document alone (unknown; our reading: not settled here) — it does not reference or amend M-25-21.

**Key content for artificial intelligence / machine-learning assurance.**
- [p.1] Sec. 1-2: States policy to pursue "a minimally burdensome national policy framework for AI" and names a Colorado "algorithmic discrimination" law as an example of state regulation it says "may even force AI models to produce false results."
- [p.1] Sec. 3: Directs the Attorney General to establish an "AI Litigation Task Force" within 30 days of the order "whose sole responsibility shall be to challenge State AI laws inconsistent with the policy set forth in section 2."
- [p.2] Sec. 4: Directs the Secretary of Commerce to publish, within 90 days, an evaluation identifying state AI laws that "require AI models to alter their truthful outputs."
- [p.2] Sec. 5: Directs a Commerce Policy Notice making states with flagged AI laws ineligible for non-deployment Broadband Equity Access and Deployment (BEAD) funds, and directs agencies to consider conditioning discretionary grants on states not enforcing such laws.
- [p.2] Sec. 6-7: Directs the FCC (Federal Communications Commission) to consider a federal AI reporting/disclosure standard preempting state law, and the FTC (Federal Trade Commission) to issue a policy statement on when state-mandated alteration of AI outputs is preempted by the FTC Act.
- [p.3] Sec. 8: Directs a legislative recommendation for a uniform federal AI framework, explicitly carving out state authority over child-safety protections, AI compute/data-center infrastructure permitting, and state government procurement and use of AI.
- No role assignment regarding a Chief AI Officer, "high-impact AI," or minimum/required risk-management practices was found anywhere in this order (per a text search of the public order); it is a federal-preemption policy order, not an agency AI-governance document.
- AI touchpoints found by a text search of the public order: the order's whole subject is AI regulation, but entirely at the level of which government may regulate AI outputs and models — no mention of "machine learning," "autonom...," "neural," "algorithm" (beyond the one Colorado-law reference above), or any system-level technical detail.

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** No direct counterpart on the current NASA document list; federal agency policy and NASA's own internal directives are separate coverage areas (our reading) — the nearest topical neighbor would be NPD 8700.1F (NASA's top-level safety and mission success policy directive), only in the loose sense that both are top-level policy statements rather than technical requirements; it answers a different question (NASA's internal safety policy vs. which government level may regulate AI at all).
